# The 2026 draft: Shoyer bought low, and the champion is sixth

*Every number here comes from `static/data/draft-2026.json`, generated by
`npm run derive-draft-report`. Picks are graded against the market as it stood on August 22,
the day before the draft — not against what we know now. Rankings use live player values as
of September 8.*

---

Ten managers spent thirteen rounds on August 23 rearranging a league that had just finished
handing Malcolm Stolarski a title. Sixteen days later, the market thinks six of them did a
better job than he did.

## Kevin Shoyer won the draft before it started

Shoyer opens the season with the most valuable starting eight in the league, and it is not
close in the way you would expect. His starters are worth 39,330 against Brenden Brown's
39,278 — a 52-point gap, which is a rounding error. The separation is underneath: Shoyer's
bench is worth 7,449, the deepest in the league.

He got there without spending a pick. Puka Nacua was kept in the twelfth round while the
market rated him the fifth-most valuable player in football, and Chase Brown was kept in the
tenth at overall rank 13. Together with the rest of his roster, Shoyer's keeper decisions
returned 196 picks of surplus, more than anyone else in the league.

That is the whole story of the 2026 keeper class, really. The players who moved the needle
were not drafted at all.

| Kept at | Player | Manager | Market rank |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Round 12 | Puka Nacua | Kevin Shoyer | 5 |
| Round 11 | De'Von Achane | Brenden Brown | 10 |
| Round 12 | Trey McBride | Garrett Cheadle | 23 |
| Round 12 | Nico Collins | Brenden Brown | 25 |
| Round 10 | Chase Brown | Kevin Shoyer | 13 |

Brenden Brown is right behind him on the same strategy — De'Von Achane in the eleventh and
Nico Collins in the twelfth, 186 picks of surplus, second only to Shoyer.

And for the first time since 2023, nobody got creative with the rules: all twenty keepers
cost exactly what Section 4 says they should. The all-time record is now 91 of 95 clean, and
all four exceptions remain in 2024 and 2025.

## The draft itself was a run on running backs, twice

This league drafts to a pattern. Six running backs in round one is normal — the 2023–25
average is 6.33. What was not normal happened in rounds two and seven.

Round two took five running backs against a three-year average of 2.67. Round seven took
six against an average of 2.67, and exactly one wide receiver against an average of 4.33.
Somebody started a run and eight people followed it.

The single best pick of the day was Tucker Harris taking Ashton Jeanty at pick 28. Jeanty
was the fourth-most valuable running back on the board and he was the fourteenth one taken
— ten spots of value that nobody else wanted to reach for.

The most expensive was at the very top. Jonah Cartwright used pick 2 on Derrick Henry, the
second running back off the board, when the market had him eighth. Henry is the back who
carried Malcolm Stolarski through both playoff rounds last season, including 45.6 in the
title game, which is exactly the kind of thing that gets a 32-year-old drafted a round
earlier than he should be.

A note on method, because it changes the answer: these are graded *within position*. Scored
against overall value instead, the steals table comes back seven-eighths quarterbacks, which
tells you nothing about this draft and everything about the fact that quarterbacks are cheap
to trade for and all ten of us still have to start one.

## Preseason rankings, and where the market is probably wrong

| # | Manager | Starters | Career | Where history ranks them |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Kevin Shoyer | 39,330 | 43-25 (.632) | 1st |
| 2 | Brenden Brown | 39,278 | 27-24 (.529) | 4th |
| 3 | Michael Streinz | 37,504 | 36-32 (.529) | 5th |
| 4 | Tucker Harris | 36,809 | 40-28 (.588) | 2nd |
| 5 | Kanoa Gilliland | 34,410 | 29-37 (.439) | 8th |
| 6 | Malcolm Stolarski | 33,036 | 31-35 (.470) | 7th |
| 7 | Paul Slaats | 32,107 | 32-36 (.471) | 6th |
| 8 | Garrett Cheadle | 30,701 | 40-28 (.588) | 3rd |
| 9 | Jonah Cartwright | 29,255 | 26-38 (.406) | 9th |
| 10 | Tyson-Jay Saena | 28,340 | 23-39 (.371) | 10th |

Two things stand out.

The first is Shoyer, who is first on both lists. He has the best roster and the best record
in league history, and he has already won this thing once. There is no argument available.

The second is Garrett Cheadle, and it is the biggest disagreement on the board — five places
of it. The market puts him eighth. Four seasons of results put him third: 40-28, a .588 win
percentage tied with Tucker Harris for the second-best in league history, and the best
regular season anybody ran last year at 12-3. He also kept Trey McBride in the twelfth
round, 92 picks of surplus and the third-best keeper decision anyone made. He went 12-3 and
finished third. The market has looked at all of that and given him the eighth-best starting
eight.

And the reigning champion is sixth. Malcolm Stolarski's starting eight is worth 33,036,
which is 6,294 short of Shoyer's, and his career record of 31-35 is the fourth-worst in the
league. He won anyway last year. That is either a warning about how much preseason roster
value is worth, or a warning about Malcolm. It has been both before.

Week one starts tomorrow.
